THE SALFORD ELECTION. The Lancashire boroughs so highly prized and so eloquently praised by the Prime Minister during the period of what was nicknamed the Conservative Reaction, seem destined to undergo another political ordeal which, judging by what hoe lately happened in the borough of Oldham, scarcely promises Ito afford so much satisfaction to Lord Bea- ' consfield as the previous ordeal afforded to Mr. Meeseli. In fact, even sanguine Con- eervatives most admit that appearances favor the oonclusion that the popularity of tl e 'Government is unmistakably on the wane. Manchester and Burnley placed some ominous handwriting on the wall of Parlia- ment, add only ths other day the borough of I Oldham having rid itself of a political super- stition whieh was made reepeotable by its , I chivalrous origin, returned to its ancient radio,' allegiance. The late Mr. Cobbett was an eminently pleasant and honorable I Igentleman, but none the less a reminiemine. of forty years ago and neither more 11., lea than a Parliamentary phantom. Oldham, relieved at last of a burdensome political inheritance, sent Mr. Hibbert to the House of Commons to suggest to the Premier that ,it endorsed the views of Manchester and Burnley, that in point of fact, the other Re- action had decidedly begun. A similar I optortunity hais rapidly come to the turn of another Lancashire borough. Salford is, at I this moment, in the throes of a noble and inspiring political oonfliat A gentleman from Bury—Colonel 0. 0. I Walker, is contesting the meat in the Con- Hiervative interest and Mr. Joseph Kay, , who fought gallantly in the same borough 1 for the Liberals, has been chosen to bear the Liberal message to Bt. Stephen's. Mr Kay ' has earned distinction as an author on guise. tions relating to land—a subject which see sion after session is moving more nearly and surely towards the sphere of Parliamentary controversy. Salford entered on its great brief campaign on Monday last, and the town is alive with that excitement which does so much to ennoble the political life of England, and to rescue it from the withering indifference which is as the death of patriotism. Since Monday meetings have been held in the borough by the supporters of both candidates, and the Liberal party asp daily, seems to be animated with ex traordinary confidence and enthusiasm. Although at first sight the battle f r an absent candidate seems wanting in the element of personal force and the inspiration of a living presence, the chivalry which ani- mates the troops of a wounded general, will doubtless afford compensating accessione of generous energy. Next Thursday, when the polling will proclaim to England that Salford is itself again, there seems good ground for anticipating that another Lan- , eaehire borough will have followed the ex- I ample of Munched.; of Burnley, and of ' Oldham.

?ammo° 1 is a name that once had a terrible sound in many • Lancashire home, and it cannot be mentioned even now with- out some feeling of indignation. When the great was °lobed in 1815 people who had I struggled and starved during the leng &ea. y period of disordered trade, high prices, com- mercial disasters, looked for an immediate return of prosperity. With peace should come plenty and good trade. But these blessings came slowly, and the people wondered why it was so. They forgot, or did not know, that the commercial effect. are felt after, and not during, a war. War often encourage., and artificially stimulate., some branches of trade. the farmer gets better prices for his produce, the manufac- turer is asked to supply the troops, and foreign competition is cut off ; the shipowner gets large freights and builds more ships; the iron-founder casts guns, and balls ; trade is brisk, and war is such a glorious thing! [ But when it is over it is found that this • prosperity has brought no increase, but a diminution of weath, and that in shutting out the foreigner with his competition we have also shut him out with his custom. So did our father', learn the lesson, and it brought with it discontent and clamour. Short periods of prosperity were followed by long seasons of distress, and the suffer- ings of the working °lessee were intense. It was probably never worse than in 1829. I Thus in Stockp.rt fifteen mills were stopped, ' and on an attempted reduction of ten per cent, in wages ten thousand persons were thrown out of employment. This continued for months, still there was an increase of stocks; drapers were ruined, shop-keepers were in great distress, wages continued to fall, and the year closed in deep gloom. The couses of therm "bad times" were various. The iniquitous corn-law made bread dear, and the people were too poor to buy meat ; clothing was expensive, protection did not allow trade to increase with a natural and steady growth. The people felt the injus- tice of their position and demanded reform. In the town public meetings were held, and energetic speeches were uttered ; in the country rick- burninge became almost univer- sal, and the calendar was crowded with eases Various attempts were made to reform some of the greater abuses of representation, but they came to noth ng. In 1830 Lord John hussell, as against O'Connell's pro- posal for universal suffrage, vote by ballot, and triennial Parliaments, moved to sub- Istituto other resolutions, providing for the [ enfranehisement of large towns such as ' Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, and Sheffield, and giving additional members to populous countries, avoiding any increase to the House of Commons by disfranchising some of the smaller boroughs, and restrain- I log others from sending more than one member. This proposal to disfranchise the pocket boroughs at once aroused the pre- judice, in both Houses, of those who con- sidered them as their moot valuable property. What were the claims of the great centres of industry to representation in comparison with Bewdley with its 19, Droitwieh with its 12, or Launceston with its 15 electors [ Sir Hobert Peel in the course of the debate seed: "They had to consider whether there was not, on the whole, a general represen- tation of the people in that House ; and whether the popular voice was not eulfloient- ly heard. For himself he thought that it was." At the end of the session Parliament was dissolved in consequence of the death of George IV. In the address to the throne Earl Grey expressed a hope that reform would not be deferred, like Catholic emanci- pation, until Government would be " oom• plied to yield to expediency, what they refused to emu:tide upon pricniple." This reused the Duke of Wellington, the premier, to utter a true Tory profession of faith in the representation;—" He was fully con- vinced that the °Gentry possessed, at the present moment, a legislature which answered all good purposes of legislation, and this to a greater degree than any legislature ever had answered, in any country whatever. He would go further, and say that the legislation and the system of representation possessed the entire confi- dence of the country,— eservedly possessed that confidence,—and the discussions in the legislature, had a very great influence over the opinions of the country. THE AMERICAN MEAT SUPPLY The blue fly which was said to have been sent by the First Napoleon to infest the shop of the British butcher was probably not half so troublesome a creature as that which now tomes every week buzzing in his ear shout the counties.) quarters of beef from America. We cannot say of the Americans that they give 'no quarter," for the quar- ters they give are becoming innumerable. Although a diminished quantity ot American meat arrived in Liverpool last week, the supply having been reduced one half, very large quantities were imported on Tues- day last, consisting of upwards of 9,000 quarters of beef and nearly 800 sheep. The following day an additional 1770 quar- ters of beef arrived, together with 850 sheep Nor is the supply now confined to the port of Liverpool. At the port of Bristol, on Mon- day, 800 quarters of beef arrived in excellent condition. The experiment of an American moat supply is being prosecuted with a vigour that promises to effect important changes in the English meat market in all its ramifications, and the experiment—for as yet it has not &deemed beyond that preli- minary stage—will be watched by the consumer, the grazier and the owner of the land with the keenest interest.

Sum writing the above, the means of transport for this precious and much coveted commodity seem likely to receive extraor- dinary extension. It is stated that the owners of the Great Eastern are comidering the propriety of converting that magnificent reseal into a huge refrigerating chamber for the conveyance of American meat. A recent examination has disclosed the fact that, like the Great Britain —another of Brunel's ships—the hull is pra ideally in as good condition as when firet built, and the direc- tors consider it would be wise to raise sufficient money to put new and improved engines and boilere into the vessel. They have been empowered to prepare a rough estimate of the cost of new machinery, and in view of the fact that the vessel can even now steam as fast as any of the Atlantic liners, the trade in meat, which is being developed not only with the United States, but also with Brazil, promises to open a wide field of usefulness—a trade in which the ' great vessel need never carry only half a load. It may be remembered that in a recent address on the subject of the Amen- pan meat supply and its probable , Peat on the English farmer and the landlord, CV G. W. Latham urged very reasinably that the chemist and the shipowner would every day render the transport of dead meat to the country more and more practicable. It would seem that they are already doing it. Even as we write "the cry is still they ' come." The latest news from Liverpool states that the quantity of fresh meat which arrived in that port from America, the week ending the 7.h ult., is considered to be the largest that has yet arrived in a similar period previously. There were five consign- ments amounting in all to 7,191 quarters of beef and 1,573 whole sheep, one consign- ment arriving on Saturday in the Guion steamer Dakota, and comprising 2,300 quarters of beef and 500 cheep. The trade in American live stock is now engaging the attention of breeders and others, and the Pioneer steamer, with a large consignment of live male, is expected shortly to arrive at Liverpool. We may remark in conclusion that, according to official statistics, 6,707,000 lbs. fresh beef were exported from New York and Philadelphia to England during Marsh, making 30,000,0001b5. during the last nine months.
